cases.abstract: DROID combines a distributed manipulation dataset with a portable collection platform to gather demonstrations across varied scenes. The shared Franka Panda setup supports reproducible control across 13 institutions; portability, randomized task assignment, and prompts to vary scene conditions broaden collection coverage. The dataset contains 76,000 successful episodes with language annotations; unsuccessful trajectories are also released but excluded from co-training. Utility is evaluated with separate diffusion policies for six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware. With a common policy backbone, in-domain-only training is compared against 50/50 co-training using either successful DROID trajectories or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. DROID co-training exceeds the next-best method in across-task mean success rate by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 percentage points on task-specific out-of-distribution variants. A count-matched subset comparison also favors broader scene diversity on the challenging shifted tasks studied. These results support the dataset's utility alongside in-domain demonstrations on the evaluated hardware and tasks.
cases.methods: DROID uses a shared, portable Franka Panda platform with external and wrist stereo cameras and VR teleoperation, allowing scene changes on a reproducible robot setup. For each new scene, collectors calibrate cameras and specify feasible tasks, from which the task for each episode is randomly sampled. Periodic prompts ask collectors to vary camera placement, lighting, clutter, or base position to broaden coverage rather than favor easy tasks. Crowdsourced annotators provide up to three independent language instructions per episode. To evaluate the data, separate language-conditioned diffusion policies are trained for six tasks across four locations on DROID hardware. Training uses a common backbone and either in-domain demonstrations alone or 50/50 co-training with successful DROID trajectories or a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. Tests use ten rollouts per method and task setting, covering perturbed in-distribution starts and task-specific out-of-distribution variants with new objects, distractors, or shifted cameras.
cases.results: With the policy backbone held fixed, DROID co-training yields higher across-task mean success rates than in-domain-only training or co-training with a curated Open X-Embodiment mixture. Each co-training mixture contains equal parts in-domain and auxiliary data, with the DROID portion restricted to successful trajectories. Across six tasks in four locations on DROID hardware, its mean success rate exceeds the next-best comparator by 22 percentage points in-distribution and 17 on task-specific out-of-distribution variants, with ten rollouts per method and task setting. A separate comparison uses 7,362 successful demonstrations per subset in 50/50 in-domain co-training. Policies co-trained with a uniformly sampled, more scene-diverse subset perform better than those using a subset from the 20 most represented scenes on the challenging shifted tasks studied. Fixing the demonstration count supports a role for scene diversity beyond quantity, although other differences between the subsets are not fully isolated.

notes.abstract: Selected D01-D03 and D05-D08 to connect reproducible, varied collection with data utility. Read-back preserves both dataset and platform, keeps the next-best comparison on six tasks with a shared backbone, and presents scene diversity as supporting evidence rather than an isolated cause.
notes.methods: D01-D03 (Section III) support the collection-to-annotation sequence; D05-D07 (Section V) anchor policy training and evaluation. Read-back makes scene variation operational, restricts DROID co-training to successful trajectories, and attaches ten rollouts to each main method and task setting.
notes.results: D06-D08 (Section V; Figs. 8 and 10) support the shared-backbone comparison and count-matched diversity check. Read-back retains equal co-training mixtures, distinguishes percentage-point gains from relative gains, and leaves the next-best comparator unspecified. The subset finding does not isolate diversity from every other difference.

cases.abstract: SIMPLER provides a simulated evaluation framework for robot policies trained on real data, targeting relative performance rather than exact real-world success rates. To reduce control mismatch, it replays actions from existing real demonstrations in simulation and tunes controller parameters against recorded end-effector trajectories. Visual Matching addresses appearance by compositing simulated robots and interactive objects with inpainted real-scene backgrounds and adjusting their textures. These procedures are implemented in SAPIEN task setups for Google Robot and WidowX. Mean Maximum Rank Violation penalizes policy misordering by real-world success-rate margins, complementing Pearson correlation. Across six policy checkpoints and three Google Robot task groups, average rank violation is 0.056 for Visual Matching, 0.143 for Variant Aggregation over randomized visual environments, and 0.375 for validation action mean squared error. Simulation also indicates greater arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, a relative difference supported by subsequent real robot arm-wrapping experiments. The results support comparative policy evaluation and behavioral diagnosis in the tested, mainly rigid-body settings.
cases.methods: To align controller action effects, SIMPLER replays actions from existing real demonstrations in SAPIEN implementations of Google Robot and WidowX tasks. It compares real and simulated end-effector translation and rotation, then uses simulated annealing to tune controller stiffness and damping; this step requires no new demonstrations. Visual Matching tackles the visual gap by compositing segmented simulated robots and interactive objects with inpainted real backgrounds and adjusting textures. Alternatively, Variant Aggregation randomizes visual environments and averages policy outcomes across them. Existing generalist policies are evaluated in paired real and simulated settings. Mean Maximum Rank Violation penalizes pairs that simulation misorders using their real-world success-rate margins: it takes each policy's worst such margin and averages across policies. Lower values indicate better ranking agreement; Pearson correlation provides a complementary measure.
cases.results: Visual Matching agrees more closely with real-world policy ordering than Variant Aggregation or validation action mean squared error in the Google Robot comparison. Across six checkpoints and three task groups, average Mean Maximum Rank Violation is 0.056, 0.143, and 0.375, respectively. This metric penalizes misordering by real-world success-rate margins, so the lower value favors Visual Matching as a ranking signal. Corresponding mean Pearson correlations are 0.924, 0.778, and 0.308; linear agreement and margin-aware ordering therefore favor the same approach. A complementary behavioral check asks whether simulated visual sensitivity appears on hardware: simulation indicates greater arm-texture sensitivity in Octo-Base than RT-1-X, and new real robot arm-wrapping experiments support that relative difference. These findings support relative performance evaluation and policy-specific visual sensitivity analysis in the tested robot setups.

notes.abstract: S01-S05 connect the evaluation target to control alignment, visual composition, and margin-aware ranking; S07 and S09 supply comparative and behavioral evidence. Read-back retains an evaluation framework rather than a new policy, scopes the numerical comparison to Google Robot task groups, and distinguishes relative agreement from exact success rates.
notes.methods: Selected S02-S06 to explain how control and appearance alignment feed paired evaluation. Read-back separates controller tuning from policy training, preserves the worst-margin-then-average metric, and identifies randomized visual aggregation as an alternative to Visual Matching. No new demonstrations are required for controller identification.
notes.results: S07 (Table I) supports the ranking comparison; S09 (Figs. 8-9) anchors the physically checked sensitivity prediction. Read-back shows that correlation and margin-aware ranking favor the same approach, while arm wrapping checks a specific relative sensitivity. The numerical values remain agreement measures, not robot success rates.
